The reason I can safely say this is that even though ostensibly the two technologies seem quite similar, they have very little in common. The reason VR is relevant is 'presence'. People who have not used the hardware generally just equate presence with immersion. As in you watched a great movie or read a great book and Wow, that was totally immersive! It's not. Presence is a very poorly understand phenomena whereby your body (and mind) physically believe they're in a different location. There is ongoing academic research to try to understand what causes this effect. It's strange and amazing. It makes VR something like a digital drug in that you're actually physically changing your body's perception of reality.

This the reason you've seen countless companies going from having next to no interest in VR given the dead sales of the ostensibly similar 3D TV to willing to dump billions in development of it. Once you try it it becomes clear that any comparison to 3D TV or frankly any entertainment technology to date is nothing short of absurd. It's going to revolutionize not just entertainment but digital interactivity. It opens up exciting possibilities for training, education, treatment, and so on. As we further evolve the haptic technologies (here's a neat concept), which in many ways are a sister technology, the possibilities become mind boggling.

There are a couple of reasons 3D TVs haven't taken off.

There's more to making games work in VR than just "making them 3D".

One of the big differences is that in most games you move in the direction you are looking. When you can look by moving your head, this doesn't make sense any more. You have to change the control scheme completely.

On top of that there's nausea issues. You can't get away with screen tearing, framerate drops or input lag without making people sick. That's aside from the fact that you half your normal FPS when you render it for VR, because you need to render from two (slightly) different viewpoints. A lot of games run on 30-45 FPS, half of which is 15-25. which is not acceptable.

There's a lot of other issues you need to worry about, but just to make sure people can move around and not throw up, these are the biggies.

Frame rates and such aside, there's also nausea inducing issues simply by having in-world acceleration which isn't happening in the real world. This would be the case for any first-person movement experience that isn't especially adapted to vr. I didn't see anyone mention what I believe is the biggest difference between 3DTV and Virtual Reality: Virtual Reality is interactive while 3DTV is not. The fact that you sit and watch television and have no control over the point of view means that 3D isn't immersive; it doesn't feel like what it should feel like. Virtual Reality, on the other hand, is inherently a bifocal experience, a 3D experience. When you get to control where you're looking and where you're moving to, when you're able to take a quick peek behind you or glance around a corner, having anything but 3D would be unusual.

The comparison might be something akin to viewing art in a museum. 3DTV would be the art on the walls. You look at the art to see the art. The artists may paint it in such a way that bring out the three-dimensional details or forces a perspective, but you're still consuming what the artist intends--And that's okay! That's how art is now. On the other hand, Virtual Reality would be like taking a trip to the museum. Having a pre-recorded, video walkthrough of a museum is a totally different and unfulfilling experience than actually going there and viewing the art first-hand. The author shouldn't be arguing that going to the museum is the same thing as having holographic art. They're apples and oranges. I think the author is off-base.

The author has a point when it comes to the majority of game genres. I don't think this is going to significantly improve on FPS or first-person games in general, and obviously it is useless for third person games.

But there are some gaming genres where VR works really well. Flight simulators in particular have always struggled with letting the player look around in a way that is not completely disorienting. Tons of different things have been tried, from simply hitting a key to change where you are looking, to "padlock views" that slew the camera all over the place, to switching to a third-person perspective when following an object. None of those are satisfactory at all.

A VR headset is a fantastic solution to this; you can track an object outside of your airplane's 90 degree forward FOV with the goggles, and then look back at your instrument panel on the screen. You maintain the feeling that the screen is the reference that is the "front" of the airplane, and the headset lets you look all around it you.

So while I don't think VR is going to be all that huge, it is definitely going to find application in some genres, like space flight games and flight sims.

Well... I'm a 25-year old somebody who lately is convincing themselves more and more that they have no actual talent in anything and may possibly be going nowhere. Yet, still I hold on to a little glimmer of hope that they could become something great but just don't know how to get there. Any advice, oh ye RandomMotivator??

Well to begin, why are you telling yourself you have no talent? You're able to walk, talk, and use a computer correctly. That's a small talent that some people can't even do. You are alive and healthy enough to function as well and can probably start on your achievements. You're 25 with the possibility of living 75 more years. Think about that, 75 years is 27,393 days from now which means there is 1,643,580 minutes until then. In those minutes you can accomplish SO MANY things! It's about starting small and taking the steps slowly.

First step, that's the hardest, is accepting who you are and your current self with your limits. What you do with this acceptance is ask yourself, what can I do to change that? In your case for talent, you have to go find it. The best way to find your calling/talent is to try many different hobbies. Dancing, programming, fitness, photography, writing, tennis, basketball, etc. and you'll eventually find something you enjoy and become good at.

If you tell yourself you're going nowhere, you need to stop telling yourself you're going nowhere but rather, you're going somewhere but you haven't found it yet. Changing something from a no to a maybe is even a step up. I was in your shoes a couple of years ago and my friend even told me that even though I said, "I don't know what to do with my life and I'm going to end up failing at it", here I am in today's present and achieving things I never thought was possible from me.

It's about getting started NOW on anything and keeping yourself busy. If you keep yourself busy, you won't have time to think of any negatives. You need to focus on the now and improving on your goals and hobbies in the moment, not worrying about the future. Your choices change your future and only you have that ability. You probably have a list of things you want to start doing or have wanted to for years now. Go start it now! Look up tutorials on youtube or google on how to start and you'll be moving in no time!
